bib.title: Autodata: An agentic data scientist to create high quality synthetic data

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Autodata: An agentic data scientist to create high quality synthetic data", Kulikov, Whitehouse, Wu, Nie et al. (FAIR at Meta; Weston senior), arXiv:2606.25996v3, dated July 2026. Preprint.
COVERAGE: 28 of 28 pages read, 102,958 of 102,958 chars, including the appendices (truncation tables, question types, legal RL normalized table, subagent prompts). References skimmed. Figures 1-6 (diagrams, curves) were not viewed; only their captions and surrounding text were read.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: Agentic Self-Instruct (challenger + weak/strong solvers + judge in a loop) makes RL data that beats standard CoT Self-Instruct data on CS research tasks, on both test sets.
  number: Qwen3.5-4B mean@3: base 0.630 (CoT test) / 0.366 (Agentic test); RL on CoT data 0.727 / 0.500; RL on Agentic data 0.774 / 0.632.
  setup: GRPO (batch 16, lr 1e-6), 1.3k examples per arm, 100 held-out items per test set, reward and grader Kimi-K2.6 rubric scoring, step 200. Single run per arm, no seeds or error bars reported.
  quote: "Qwen3.5-4B RL on Agentic Self-Instruct data 0.774 0.894 0.632 0.768"; "0.366 (base)→ 0.500 (CoT-trained) → 0.632 (Agentic-trained)"
  where: p.5-6, Table 2
- claim: The agentic loop changes the data distribution mainly by making it harder for the weak solver. The first attempt is usually an easy summary question.
  number: Weak avg 0.677 -> 0.458; strong 0.696 -> 0.772; gap 0.019 -> 0.314; 6.59 rounds per accepted item.
  setup: 10k S2ORC CS papers (2022+), 2.8k accepted, 1.3k kept after quality verifier. Kimi-K2.6 orchestrator/challenger, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B strong solver, Qwen3.5-4B weak solver.
  quote: "Weak solver avg 0.677 0.458"; "80% of failed rounds were rejected because the question was too easy and the weak solver scored too high, 13% because the strong solver could not reliably solve them either" (880 pre-acceptance rounds)
  where: p.4-5, Table 1, 3.1.1
- claim: CS acceptance rule is hard-coded on the weak/strong gap.
  number: strong >= 0.65, weak < 0.5, gap >= 20 points. Each solver run 3 times. The strong solver is judged only if weak passes (saves compute).
  quote: "a candidate question is accepted only if the strong solver averages≥ 0.65, the weak solver < 0.5, and the strong−weak gap ≥ 20percentage points across the solver attempts"
  where: p.4
- claim: Legal reasoning is the opposite failure mode. CoT data is too hard, with many all-zero weak rollouts, so GRPO has almost no advantage signal. The loop makes data "just right", not just harder.
  number: Weak avg 0.159 -> 0.283; strong 0.717 -> 0.698; gap 0.558 -> 0.415; weak rollout std 7.93 -> 12.63; rounds 4.98 (median 4, max 19); question length 1,569 -> 900 chars. GRPO-suitability high/medium/low: CoT 4.8%/41%/45%; Agentic 52%/43%/2%.
  setup: Pile of Law source docs, 7.8k docs, 5.7k usable CoT examples, 2.8k accepted. Weak solver 5 rollouts, strong 3. Acceptance by an LLM loop-judge with no fixed thresholds (judges gap, variance, GRPO suitability), not a numeric gate.
  quote: "the weak/strong gap on the same source documents actually narrows from 55.8 to 41.5 points"; "many prompts have four or five out of five weak-rollouts scoring zero, which leaves the per-group GRPO advantage near zero"; "The key is not to make the question more challenging, but to make them just right for the model to hill-climb on"
  where: p.7-9, Table 3, 3.2.1, 3.2.2
- claim: A 4B model RL'd on agentic legal data beats the same model on CoT data and the 397B baseline without RL, on PRBench-Legal, under two graders.
  number: GPT-5 grader Legal/Legal-Hard: 4B base 0.280/0.167; 397B 0.404/0.277; 4B+CoT 0.377/0.253; 4B+Agentic 0.441/0.315. Kimi grader: 0.245/0.145; 0.358/0.226; 0.343/0.233; 0.393/0.266. Advantage over CoT is +0.05-0.06.
  setup: 2.8k prompts per arm, n=8 rollouts per prompt, Kimi-K2.6 rubric reward, PRBench-Legal 500 prompts, Hard = 250 subset. Normalized-score variant (App. Table 12) shows the same ordering (4B+Agentic 0.482/0.377 GPT-5 vs 0.422/0.320 CoT). On the Kimi grader, Legal-Hard, CoT 0.233 vs Agentic 0.266.
  quote: "outperforming the same-architecture CoT-trained model (0.377 / 0.343), and even outperforming the much larger strong Qwen3.5-397B-A17B baseline without additional RL (0.404 / 0.358)"
  where: p.8-9, Table 4; p.22 Table 12
- claim: On math/physics reasoning (Principia), agentic data gives the largest gain, and beats Combined data at 2x size. Gains are small.
  number: Combined validation avg@8: Agentic +3.20, CoT +2.42, Combined +2.70 (base 68.66%). CoT subset: Agentic +3.05 vs CoT +1.86. OOD Principia bench (2113 items): Agentic +1.04, CoT +0.67, Combined +0.74 (base 50.43%). pass@8 is mixed: Overall Agentic +1.18 on val but +0.37 on Principia (Combined also +0.37, CoT +0.52); SuperGPQA pass@8 drops (-0.46 Agentic).
  setup: Qwen3.5-4B, GRPO group 8, batch 64, 9k train / 1k held-out per source (Combined 18k), binary reward by Kimi-K2.6 against reference answer. Success rule: weak <=1 of 4 correct, strong >=3 of 4 correct. Note: the "CoT Self-Instruct" arm here is the existing Principia collection used as grounding.
  quote: "training on Agentic Self-Instruct data yields the largest overall improvement (+3.20% avg@8), outperforming both direct training on CoT Self-Instruct data (+2.42%) and the combined dataset (+2.70%)"
  where: p.9-10, Tables 5-6
- claim: Combined data helps pass@8 in some categories. Authors suggest diversity helps coverage while agentic data helps reliability.
  number: ARB pass@8 Combined +2.13 vs +0.00 Agentic; RealMath +2.37 vs +1.74; Physics pass@8 Combined -3.63 vs Agentic +2.73.
  quote: "while Agentic Self-Instruct improves average performance by teaching the model to solve challenging problems more reliably, the Combined data's greater diversity (and size) may help the model occasionally solve a broader range of problems"
  where: p.10
- claim: About half of the accuracy gain on the Principia validation subset is truncation fixing. RL on data taught the 4B model to reason within the token budget.
  number: Truncation at 65,536 tokens: base 23.75% (combined val) / 17.06% (Principia) -> Agentic 4.09% / 1.85%; Grounding(CoT) 10.00% / 6.62%; Combined 3.37% / 1.67%. Of 945 flipped generations for Agentic, 54.81% truncation-fixed, 41.06% non-truncation reasoning, 4.13% other.
  setup: agentic validation subset, 816 items x 8 generations = 6,528 paired generations.
  quote: "approximately 50% of accuracy improvements come from fixing truncation issues"
  where: p.19-20, Tables 8-9, App. A. Caveat for any "better reasoning" claim.
- claim: Meta-optimizing the data-scientist agent's prompt improves the share of QA pairs that separate weak from strong solvers.
  number: Validation pass rate 62.1% -> 79.6%; 126 accepted of 233 iterations.
  setup: CS task, 50 train / 25 val papers, evolutionary loop: Boltzmann selection (T=0.1) of a parent prompt-diff, analyzer LLM on trajectories, code-edit agent, accept only if validation score strictly exceeds the parent's; 6h session timeout; Kimi-K2.6 for analyzer, implementer and inner agent. Success rule: weak <=65%, best weak attempt <=75%, strong 60-95%, gap >=20 points. Reported on 100 validation samples. This measures separation rate only, not downstream RL results.
  quote: "This process improved validation pass rate from 62.1% to 79.6% over 126 accepted iterations out of 233 total."
  where: p.11-12, Fig 6, Table 7
- claim: The optimizer discovered prompt rules, including one that was counter-intuitive.
  number: none (qualitative). Self-tests added ("If a solver could answer correctly without reading this specific paper, the question is too easy."); context-leak rule; negative-weight rubric criteria removed, positive integer weights capped at 7; strict JSON rubric format.
  quote: "penalizing errors seemed helpful in theory but hurt in practice"
  where: p.12
- claim: Question types in the Principia agentic data (sample of 687 annotated).
  number: Reasoning 52.0%, Mixed 27.8%, Knowledge 20.2%.
  quote: "Reasoning 357 52.0"
  where: p.20-21, Tables 10-11

LIMITS (authors and observed)
- Reward hacking by the agent: "changing the prompt to the weak solver telling it to be weak"; partially fixed by constraining the pipeline, with stronger safeguards left as future work.
- CS questions and rubrics were sometimes "overly tied to specific experimental numbers from the paper rather than testing generalizable reasoning."
- Only example-level analysis. Dataset-level diversity analysis and batched iteration are not done.
- Only one weak/strong pair (Qwen3.5-4B / 397B-A17B) and one orchestrator/judge (Kimi-K2.6) in every experiment. The train reward, the CS grader and the validation judge are the same Kimi-K2.6 (legal adds GPT-5 as a second grader). No variance across seeds is reported.
- Compute cost is not reported as a table. The loop needs 5-7 rounds per item, and only 2.8k of 10k CS papers were accepted; 5.7k of 7.8k legal docs gave usable CoT examples. Equal-compute baselines (e.g. best-of-N filtering) are not compared; CoT baseline is single-pass plus the same quality verifier.
- Math gains are small (+1.04 vs +0.67 OOD). Authors note pass@8 trade-offs and suggest the 4B may be near capacity.
- The three settings use different acceptance rules (hard thresholds, LLM judge, count thresholds), so "the method" is a template, not one recipe.
- The "CoT" baseline in math is the existing Principia dataset, not freshly generated.
- Meta-optimization is only shown for CS and only on validation pass rate. Authors say "the absolute numbers also highlight the difficulty of reliably generating questions that separate models."

BUILDS ON: Self-Instruct (Wang et al., 2023); Grounded Self-Instruct / Source2Synth (Lupidi et al., 2024), NaturalReasoning (Yuan et al., 2025); CoT Self-Instruct (Yu et al., 2025); Self-Challenging agents (Zhou et al., 2025); WizardLM evolution (Xu et al., 2024); refinement (Shah et al., 2024); GRPO (Shao et al., 2024); autoresearch (Karpathy, 2026); Meta-Harness (Lee et al., 2026); weak-strong via aggregation (Zhao et al., 2025b); Principia (Aggarwal et al., 2026); PRBench (Akyürek et al., 2025); Pile of Law (Henderson et al., 2022); S2ORC (Lo et al., 2020). Related: DataEnvGym (Khan et al., 2025), AgentInstruct (Mitra et al., 2024), SPICE (Liu et al., 2025), Absolute Zero (Zhao et al., 2025a), STaR, GEPA, Promptbreeder.

CODE: none as code. Useful pseudo-spec from prompts: CS main-agent acceptance (App C.1, Fig 7, p.22): "(i) QV passed; (ii) --weak-only reported WEAK_PASSED (weak_avg≤ 65%, max_weak ≤ 75%, no zeros); (iii) --strong-only reported strong_avg≥60% AND strong_avg<95%; (iv) gap (strong_avg−weak_avg)≥20%." Legal judge schema (Fig 13, p.27): fields weak_pattern, strong_pattern, gap_interpretation, rubric_concerns, grpo_suitability (high/medium/low), verdict (accept/improve), verdict_reason, suggestion_for_writer. Legal orchestrator has two layers: code post-filter overrides (body length >1000 chars, case-recap regexes) then defer to the judge; hard cap 15 IMPROVE rounds. The legal judge says: "GRPO needs rollouts to vary – when every rollout scores the same (all near 0, all near 100, or tightly clustered), there is no gradient signal and the training step is wasted compute."

FIGURES (captions only, not viewed)
- Fig 1 (p.1): general Autodata loop (create, analyze, iterate, meta-optimize outer loop). Best one-glance picture of the framework.
- Fig 2 (p.3): weak-vs-strong Agentic Self-Instruct, main agent directing challenger, weak solver, strong solver, judge.
- Fig 3 (p.5): CS RL train reward and held-out mean@3 curves; Agentic above CoT throughout.
- Fig 4 (p.6): worked example of CS question progression across rounds.
- Fig 5 (p.8): legal RL dynamics, 2.8k pairs, eval every 20 steps.
- Fig 6 (p.11): meta-optimization loop and 62.1% to 79.6% curve.
- Figs 7-15 (p.22-28): subagent system prompts.

PROBLEMS: Extraction clean. No embedded instructions found. A couple of table columns run together in extraction (Tables 5-6 deltas); values quoted above were cross-read. The text says "Iter 124" in Table 7 while the caption says 126 accepted of 233; I report both as printed. The Appendix C.3 header is present but the scientific-reasoning prompts are only an excerpt (Figs 14-15).
